Acknowledgements
The World Health Organization (WHO) acknowledges the contributions of individuals and 
partner organizations to the development of Bleeding after birth: course on prevention, 
diagnosis and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage. WHO thanks Jhpiego, an international 
non-profit health organization affiliated with Johns Hopkins University, for its leadership in 
updating the Bleeding after Birth Complete 3.0 module from the Helping Mothers Survive 
programme. This updated module, led by Cherrie Lynn Evans, was developed in response 
to updated WHO recommendations and emerging evidence on the new diagnostic criteria 
for earlier diagnosis of postpartum haemorrhage. The original module was developed by 
Jhpiego’s Technical Leadership Office in collaboration with Laerdal Global Health, and built 
on the educational design of Helping Babies Breathe, created by the American Academy of 
Pediatrics and Laerdal Global Health.
The development of the technical content in this update was initiated by Susheela Engelbrecht, 
Cherrie Lynn Evans and Jennifer Stevens from Jhpiego, in collaboration with Teesta Dey and 
Ioannis Gallos from WHO Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child, Adolescent 
Health and Ageing, who ensured alignment with WHO guidelines and current evidence. 
WHO acknowledges the substantial technical contributions provided by Jolly Beyeza-
Kashesya, Anne Beatrice Kihara and Alison Wright from the International Federation of 
Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO); Jacqueline Dunkley‐Bent, Zab Frankling, Liselotte Kweekel, 
Stephanie Marriott and Kate Stringer from the International Confederation of Midwives 
(ICM); and Muna Abdullah, Manuel Couffignal, Catherine Howard Taylor, Chisato Masuda, 
Isabelle Moreira, Catrin Schulte-Hillen and Duncan Shikuku from the United Nations Population 
Fund (UNFPA). WHO also thanks Camila Barrera Daza, Bjørn Mike Boge and the Laerdal Global 
Health design team for their contributions to the educational design of the module.

(Ministry of Health, Occupied Palestinian Territory, including east Jerusalem); Ferdousi Begum

Plan and coordinate
• Coordinate with leadership and local organizers well in advance.
• Use the supplementary sample documents – like agendas, room 
layouts, checklists and evaluations. Download and modify these 
documents to fit your needs. 
• Review clinical data with facility management to identify strengths 
and gaps.
Adapt the course to the needs
This course is for all health workers who care for women at birth. All 
women should give birth in facilities with the capacity to treat PPH, 
including administration of IV medicines. 
• In facilities with no operating room and which cannot provide 
advanced care, women not responding to the PPH bundle should be 
transferred quickly. Adapt the course based on these conditions.
• Consider excluding from the course, if not available or relevant:
 
—non-pneumatic anti‐shock garment (NASG) – pages 29 and 30 
 
—uterine balloon tamponade (UBT) – page 36
 
—repairing deep vaginal and cervical tears – page 37.
• Define the agenda based on the content you will be covering.
Prepare yourself to facilitate
• Review the agenda.
• Familiarize yourself with all pages in this flipchart.
• Rehearse in advance how you will deliver the course and how you will 
best engage the participants.
• Practise each of the demonstrations and simulations. 
Set up the course for active participation
The number of participants in a course may vary, but ensure you can 
divide into small groups of 6 participants to 1 facilitator to ensure the 
quality of practice activities. 
Prepare the learning materials
In addition to this Flip Chart, use these resources to support learning and 
ensure an impactful course delivery. Make sure you know them well, and 
have them ready for the course. 
Action plans
Two large posters showing the steps to take during care, to be used 
during the course and as a job aid for clinical practice.
Provider guide
A booklet for every health worker to use during the course and keep 
afterwards, for continued practice.
Assessments
As part of the learning process, the course includes a pre‐course and 
post‐course knowledge check, and six objective structured clinical 
examinations (OSCEs). 
Videos
Demonstration videos are available to view online and download. 
Use them during the course and share with participants for continued 
Prepare to assess
• Assessments support learning and help you identify gaps and needs.
• Ensure participants complete knowledge assessments before and after 
the course.
• Check skills after the course using OSCEs. 
Enable continued practice
Support the facilities to embrace continued practice after the course.
• Make the Action Plans available and visible in the facility.
• Appoint two participants from each facility to become practice 
coordinators and support their peers.
• Ensure participants have the equipment, space and time to carry out 
low‐dose, high‐frequency (LDHF) practice at the facilities –using the 
activities in the Provider Guide.

Plan and prepare to facilitate a course
The Bleeding after birth 
training course aims to 
translate standards into care.
It incorporates the latest 
WHO recommendations 
related to PPH1,2 and includes 
links to key references and 
resources for training. 
Find all learning materials 
and supplementary sample 
documents at 
www.who.int/tools/ 
bleeding-after-birth
This course is for all health workers who care for women at birth. All women should give 
birth in facilities with the capacity to treat postpartum haemorhage (PPH), and administer 
intravenous (IV) medicines.

These sections cover key knowledge the participants will need.
• Use your own words, be concise and avoid just reading. 
• To engage participants, prepare how you will deliver explanations 
in advance.
Show participants the actions they need to take, and prepare them to 
• For some steps, videos are available. 
• Always emphasize and model respectful care and good 
communication.
Practise 
Give participants time to repeat newly learned or refreshed skills for 
each step. 
• Spend more time practicing than explaining. 
• Encourage self‐reflection and debriefing with the team. 
Encourage participants to share and explore what is done in their 
facility. Find ways to overcome barriers and put new skills into 
Ask questions to review and reinforce learning. Create a safe space 
and ensure all participants participate.
Scenario practice
Reinforce skills learned in a simulation practice. 
• Ensure every group has all the equipment on the checklist. 
• Encourage self‐reflection and feedback.
• One or two participants will take the role of health workers, 
using only the Action Plan and Postpartum Monitoring Form for 
guidance.
• Ensure the rest follow the actions on the Action Plan. Rotate 
participants on the next scenario.
• You will act as the woman, operate the simulator, give prompts 
as needed, and provide vitals and other information when 
participants asses for them.
• Alternatively, a participant could be the woman with your 
guidance.
Assess knowledge
Assess the participants’ knowledge before and after the course. 
• Use the knowledge checks available as available as supplementary 
material. Find them at www.who.int/tools/bleeding-after-birth.
• Use the results from the pre‐course test to tailor facilitation to the 
needs.
Assess skills
Assess the participants’ skills after the course using OSCEs. 
• Make sure to plan enough time to assess all participants.
• There are six OSCE cases available as supplementary material. Find 
them at www.who.int/tools/bleeding-after-birth.
For the facilitator
Using this Flip Chart to facilitate learning
The Flip Chart is a guide for the facilitator of a course. It includes all you need to facilitate 
learning in an engaging an participatory way. Place the Flip Chart with the illustration pages 
facing the participants, and the text facing you. The content is divided into sections with 
different learning methodologies, explained below.
1b

MODULE 1
Saving lives at birth
2

• There are two people who need our 
care: the woman and her newborn.
• Survival of the baby can depend on 
survival of the woman. 
• This course helps you master 
competencies to prevent, diagnose 
and treat PPH. 
• All women should give birth in facilities 
with the capacity to treat PPH and 
administer IV medicines. 
Continued learning for health 
workers
• This course is for all health workers who 
care for women at birth. 
• We will use different learning methods:
 
—discussions 
 
—demonstrations 
 
—hands‐on practice 
 
—feedback
 
—case scenarios for simulation. 
• After the course, short, frequent drills 
and other exercises at the facility will 
strengthen and maintain skills.
Learning materials
• Action Plans are for clinical training, 
drills and as a job aid: 
 
—Action Plan 1 – Prevention and early 
diagnosis of PPH
 
—Action Plan 2 – Treatment of PPH.
• Provider Guide, a personal resource for 
all participants for continued practice 
after the course. It includes:
 
—LDFH activities for quality 
inprovement.
 
—tools like medication information and 
Postpartum Monitoring Form
 
—key knowledge and references.
Role‐play (optional)
Suddenly start a role‐play interrupting the 
course.
• A woman walks into the room about to 
give birth, asking for help.
• She gives birth, but bleeds excessively 
and you cannot stop it. She dies. 
• Consider redoing this role-play at the 
end of the course and have her survive.
1. Have you ever seen someone die from 
bleeding after birth? What happened?
2. Was there anything that could have 
been done differently or if the woman 
had been somewhere else?
MODULE 1
Saving lives at birth
2
Before you start
• Have all equipment. Refer to page 1b in this flipchart.
• Prepare a co‐facilitator or volunteer participant to wear the 
simulator and act as the woman during demonstrations, 
throughout the course.
Start the course
• Begin with the pre‐course knowledge check.
• At the end of this page you may include a surprise 
role‐play of a normal birth that progresses to PPH and 
leads to death.
2b

Main causes of 
bleeding after birth
Tone
Soft uterus
Tissue
or fragments
Trauma

3

Main causes of bleeding after birth
• All women are at risk for life‐threatening 
• Be vigilant for early warning signs.
• Dangerous bleeding can be a slow, 
steady stream or a large gush. 
• Respond quickly if a woman 
has signs that PPH may be likely.
The main causes of bleeding are: 
1. Tone – accounts for about 70% of PPH 
cases
• If the uterus does not contract, blood 
continues to pump into the uterus.
• Monitor women closely. A uterus that is 
contracted can later become atonic.
• A full bladder can prevent the uterus 
from contracting.
• Risks: 
 
—large babies >4500 g
 
—previous PPH
 
—long labours
 
—shoulder dystocia
 
—anaemia
 
—multiple pregnancy.
2. Tissue – accounts for about 20% of 
PPH cases
• Tissue left behind can cause atony and 
infection.
• Tissue includes:
 
—retained placental tissue
 
—amnion
 
—blood clots
 
—placenta praevia
 
—invasive placenta.
3. Trauma – accounts for about 10% of 
PPH cases
• Includes laceration, hematoma, uterine 
inversion and rupture.
• Risks:
 
—large babies
 
—female genital mutilation
 
—episiotomies – should not be done 
routinely.
 
—augmented or obstructed labour
 
—caesarean birth
 
—vacuum or forceps birth.
4. Thrombin (coagulopathy) – accounts 
for about 1% of PPH cases
• Risks: 
 
—severe pre‐eclampsia or eclampsia
 
—disseminated intravascular 
coagulopathy
 
—placental abruption
 
—invasive placenta
 
—history of coagulopathy
 
—sepsis.
1. Who is at risk for postpartum bleeding?
 
—All women.
2. What is the most common cause of 
bleeding?
 
—Atony or a uterus that will not 
contract.

3b

 
 
 and prevent infection
4

Provide respectful care and prevent infection
• 
• All good relationships begin with 
respect and trust. 
• This is important in healthcare – people 
trust us to help them.
• During complications, respectful care 
also involves being a calming presence.
Key points for respectful care 
• Women make their own informed 
choices, even when unexpected things 
happen.
• Women feel safe and cared for.
• Women have privacy, even during an 
emergency.
• Women are enabled to have a 
companion of their choice.
Respectful communication
• Introduce yourself by name, and use 
the woman’s name.
• Inform the woman and her family 
of progress, options, and concerns 
throughout care.
• Listen without interrupting, and 
confirm you understand her.
• Explain early if transfer for advanced 
care is needed.
• Always be honest:
 
—admit if you don’t know something
 
—maintaining trust matters more than 
appearing knowledgeable.
Prevent Infection
• Wash hands and wear sterile gloves.
• Wear apron, mask, and eye shield to 
protect yourself.
• To protect the baby:
 
—wear double gloves before birth
 
—remove the soiled pair before 
clamping and cutting the cord.
• Properly dispose of or process 
contaminated supplies and equipment. 
Follow protocols. 
1. How does respectful care save lives?
2. How do you support a woman to make 
her own choices, especially when 
something unexpected happens?
3. What changes, big or small, could 
improve respectful care in your daily 
work?
4. Are there any challenges with infection 
prevention at your facility?
 
 
 and prevent infection
4
• Begin this page introducing Action Plan 1. 
• As you explain respectful care and infection prevention, 
point out were they are on the Action Plan. 
4b

Prepare for birth, 
check equipment and 
medications
 
 
5

Prepare for birth, check equipment and medications
• Preparing the woman and the bedside 
helps prevent and treat PPH.
During antenatal care (ANC) 
– address anaemia to prevent PPH
Prevent anaemia 
• Give all pregnant women:
 
—30–60 mg of elemental iron and
 
—400 μg of folic acid 
 
—see formulations on page 37 of the 
Provider Guide.
Assess for anaemia
• Full blood count (FBC) is recommended.
• If unavailable, use a haemoglobinometer (preferred over colour scale).
Address anaemia
• Increase elemental iron if haemoglobin 
(Hb) is:
 
—<11 g/dl in the 1st or 3rd trimester, or
 
—<10.5 g/dl in the 2nd trimester
• Give 120 mg elemental iron a day until 
Hb reaches ≥11 g/dl.
• Consider IV iron before labour if:
 
—iron deficiency anaemia is confirmed, 
and
 
—oral iron is not tolerated, and 
 
—rapid response is needed.
Prepare your PPH emergency kit
• Have an emergency trolley or box to 
manage complications quickly.
• Check daily if it is stocked and available. 
See page 13 of the Provider Guide for a 
list.
During labour
• Encourage frequent urination.
• Based on the woman’s preference –
reduce perineal trauma using massage, 
warm compresses, and a hands‐on 
technique to deliver the head or breech.
• Avoid episiotomies. If medically 
indicated: 
 
—use medio‐lateral incision for lower 
risk of injury to the anal sphincter.
 
—continuous suturing repair is 
preferred to interrupted sutures.
1. During ANC, how do you test for 
anaemia?
 
—Allow participants to describe 
their experience and reflect on 
recommendation.
2. At your facility, do you have all the PPH 
emergency supplies listed on page 13 of 
the Provider Guide?
 
—If no or if incomplete, recommend 
the activity of page 12 of the Provider 
Guide later at the facility.
Prepare for birth, 
check equipment and 
medications
 
 
5
5b

 
 
Use the Postpartum Monitoring Form
6

As you used the Labour Care Guide3 
during labour, use the Postpartum 
Monitoring Form to:
• Assess and record often, as you provide 
care:
 
—consider all information, history, prior 
complications and other risk factors
 
—review trends in current care. 
• Identify possible diagnosis, based on 
your assessment and records.
• Communicate and act, based on your 
diagnosis:
 
—What care does the woman need?
 
—Call a more senior health worker?
 
—Advanced care or transfer?
Assess and record repeatedly
• Before birth, fill in any risk factors 
for PPH.
• From the birth onwards, check regularly 
for signs of PPH.
• Record four times in the first hour 
after birth to help diagnose PPH quickly.
• First assessment: 
 
—when placenta is delivered, or 
 
—15 min after birth if placenta is not 
yet out
 
—this is the most critical, most PPH 
happens in the first 20 min after birth.
• Repeat every 15 min for the first hour, or 
until stable.
What should you check?
• Uterine tone.
• Volume of blood loss and flow using 
measurement tool (reviewed on next 
page).
• Blood pressure (BP) and pulse. 
Warning vital signs include: 
• Pulse >100.
• Systolic BP <100, diastolic BP <60.
• Shock index (SI) >1.
What is SI?
• Quick bedside tool to identify early 
signs of shock.
• SI = Pulse ÷ Systolic BP
• Warning. SI >1 may indicate shock.
• Example: Pulse 110 / systolic BP 100 = SI 
1.1 = warning sign
Quick rule of thumb: 
if pulse > systolic BP, then SI >1 and cause 
for warning.
Refer to the Postpartum Monitoring Form 
in Provider Guide page 8. 
• Ask participants to review the form 
quietly for 1 min
• Quickly demonstrate how to use each 
section of the form.
1. Form groups of 4 to discuss (3 min):
 
—what is familiar?
 
—what might be harder to use?
2. A person from each group shares group’s 
observations in 1 min.
 
 
Use the Postpartum Monitoring Form
6
6b

MODULE 2
Prevention and 
early diagnosis of PPH
 
 
7

Prevent PPH 
Actively preventing PPH ensures:
 
—a shorter third stage of labour
 
—less blood loss
 
—fewer cases of PPH.
Steps to prevent and identify PPH
1. Give a uterotonic to prevent PPH in 
both vaginal and caesarean births after 
the last baby is born.
2. Place the blood measurement tool 
and monitor blood loss closely.
3. Deliver placenta with controlled 
cord traction (CCT) after clamping and 
cutting the cord.
4. Check uterine tone and massage if soft. 
Once the woman is stable
• Check the placenta for completeness. 
• Check for and repair tears.
• Assess and record tone, bleeding and 
vital signs.
• Keep the blood loss monitoring tool in 
place for the first hour for all women. If 
a woman continues to bleed, leave the 
tool in place for another hour.
Continue care for woman and baby
The time after birth is critical for both the 
woman and her baby.
• Ensure the baby is breathing well and 
kept warm.
• Keep them together and skin‐to‐skin for 
the first hour. 
• Encourage breastfeeding.
• If the baby needs resuscitation and you 
are alone:
 
—care for the baby
 
—give the uterotonic and check tone as 
soon as possible. 
If the woman arrives in your care after 
giving birth elsewhere: provide care 
based on her signs, symptoms, and any 
information about previous treatment.
1. What is the most important step to 
prevent PPH?
 
—Give a uterotonic immediately after 
the last baby is born.
2. Do you check the placenta for 
completeness immediately after birth?
 
—No. Always check uterine tone and 
bleeding first. If the uterus is firm and 
there is no bleeding, then closely 
examine the placenta.
MODULE 2
Prevention and 
early diagnosis of PPH
 
 
7
• Point to the steps for PPH prevention on Action Plan 1 as you 
explain them. 
7b

Immediately after birth, check for second baby
Give a uterotonic 
 
 
Oxytocin 10 IU IM or IV OR
Carbetocin/HSC 100 μg IM or IV OR
Misoprostol 400–600 μg PO
8

Give a uterotonic within 1 min
• What uterotonics are available in your 
facility and what is used for prevention?
• Always prepare a uterotonic before 
birth.
• Give uterotonic within 1 min after the 
last baby is born.
Never give a uterotonic before last baby 
is born. Always check for another baby.
Uterotonics for prevention
Oxytocin
• 10 international units (IU) intramuscular 
(IM) or intravenous (IV). 
• IV preferred if IV already in place: 10 IU 
diluted and given slowly over 1–2 min.
• Use and storage:
 
—can also be used for treatment
 
—WHO’s preferred choice for all 
women
 
—refrigerate (2–8°C)
 
—if cold storage can’t be guaranteed, 
use carbetocin/HSC or misoprostol.
Carbetocin and heat‐stable carbetocin 
(HSC)
• 100 μg (1 mL) IM or IV.
• If IV, administer slowly over 1 min.
• Use and storage:
 
—only for prevention of PPH 
 
—never for induction or augmentation, 
can cause uterine rupture
 
—carbetocin – refrigerate (2–8°C) 
 
—HSC – no refrigeration needed, 
protect from light.
Misoprostol
• 400–600 μg orally (PO) sublingually (SL) 
or per rectum (PR) based on woman’s 
preference.
• Use and storage:
 
—no refrigeration needed 
 
—protect from humidity
 
—for prevention and treatment.
Do not use for prevention of PPH: TXA, 
injectable prostaglandin, or ergometrine 
alone or in combination with oxytocin.
Special considerations for women at 
high risk of PPH
• Some women are at high risk of PPH 
– if they have anaemia, prior PPH, 
caesarean birth, female genital 
mutilation, sepsis, multiple pregnancy, 
placenta praevia, macrosomia with a 
birthweight of more than 4500 g, or 
shoulder dystocia.
• For women at high risk, you may use:
 
—a combination of oxytocin 10 IU IM or 
IV and misoprostol 400–600 μg PO 
 
—Find details in Provider Guide, page 6.

9

• Measure blood loss objectively to 
quickly diagnose and treat PPH.
• A blood loss measurement tool is 
recommended for all women, both for 
vaginal and caesarean births.
Blood loss measurement tools
• For vaginal birth, use a tool that:
 
—easily shows volume of blood loss 
 
—collects all blood and avoids spillage
 
—ensures the woman’s comfort and 
choice of birth position.
• Examples:
 
—drapes with a calibrated funnel
 
—trays with calibrated lines
 
—other innovations.
Place the tool
• Immediately after the baby is born and 
you have given the uterotonic. 
• For non‐supine position birth:
 
—assist her to a supine position
 
—place baby on her chest
 
—give uterotonic, then place tool.
Measure blood loss accurately
• Sweep blood and clots into the tool.
• If using a drape:
 
—hang the funnel over the edge of the 
bed, or
 
—lift the funnel so blood collects at the 
bottom.
• Check continuously to diagnose PPH 
quickly:
 
—amount of blood in the tool and 
 
—blood flow.
• First recording of blood loss volume on 
the Postpartum Monitoring Form:
 
— after the placenta delivers, or 
 
—15 min after birth if placenta is not 
out.
Prevent infection: follow protocols for 
safe disinfection, sterilisation or disposal 
of tools.
1. Place the tool
• Ask two participants to be the woman 
and the health worker, and demonstrate 
placing the tool.
• Make sure they place it correctly.
• Open blood tank to a heavy flow.
• Demonstrate how to sweep blood and 
clots into the tool.
2. Monitor blood loss
• When 300 mL blood in tool, ask a 
participant to read out the volume of 
blood lost.
• Show where to record it on the 
Postpartum Monitoring Form.
1. Have you used a blood loss measuring 
tool?
2. What was challenging when placing the 
tool and checking the blood volume?
3. What can you do to make it easier?

Blood loss assessment activity
How accurate is visual 
estimation of blood loss?
10

How accurate is visual estimation of blood loss?
Set up four stations with containers 
holding different amounts of blood, 
labelled A, B, C, D:
A. White towel or cloth, with 600 mL.
B. Gauze bandage, with 100 mL.
C. Liquid in a basin, with 300 mL.
D. Blood clot (red fruit jam), with 500 mL.
2. Read these instructions
• Go for a short break to walk by stations. 
• Estimate the blood loss at each station 
and write it down.
3. Discuss
• What were your estimates? 
• Are they different among the group?
• What are the consequences of 
underestimating? 
• Why is objective measurement of blood 
loss recommended?
4. Explain 
• The purpose of this activity is to 
create awareness of the importance of 
measuring blood loss objectively. 
• Visual estimation of blood loss is 
unreliable and may delay diagnosis and 
treatment of PPH. 
• This is why using a tool to measure 
blood loss is key to early diagnosis and 
treatment of PPH.
• Decision-making is guided by:
 
—blood loss and rate of flow
 
—uterine tone, and 
 
—the woman’s vital signs. 
• All women are at risk for life‐threatening 
• Dangerous bleeding can be:
 
—a slow, constant trickle
 
—a heavy flow 
 
—a large gush
 
—large blood clots expelled.

Be alert. If PPH, start bundle
From the moment the baby is born,

• Atonic uterus, heavy blood flow, large

—systolic BP < 100 mmHg
 
—diastolic BP < 60 mmHg
 
—SI >1.

11b

Cut the cord and

12

Cut the cord and perform controlled cord traction
Cutting the cord 
• Waiting 1–3 min to cut the cord helps 
the baby with:
 
—increased blood volume to support 
lung expansion
 
—more red blood cells to avoid 
anaemia.
• Cut immediately and get help if:
 
—the woman is bleeding heavily
 
—the baby is not breathing well.
• Use sterile or disinfected instruments. 
• Change gloves or remove outer pair if 
double‐gloved, before cutting the cord.
CCT 
• Should only be done by skilled health 
workers.
• Begin CCT after signs of placental 
separation – gush of blood or 
lengthening of the cord.
• Apply CCT only during contractions.
• Never pull hard on the cord.
• Stop if resistance is felt to avoid tearing 
off the cord and uterine inversion.
 
 Explain your actions respectfully.
 
 Prevent infection.
 
 Clamp and cut cord.
 
 Wait 1–3 min after birth if both woman 
and baby are stable.
 
 Place clamps. Cut cord between clamps.
Perform CCT
 
 Clamp the cord close to perineum.
 
 Look for signs of separation.
 
 During a contraction:
 
—gently pull down on the cord 
 
—provide counter traction just above 
the pubic bone to stabilize the uterus.
 
 Do not pull suddenly or in other 
directions.
 
 Release traction between contractions.
 
 Stop if you notice resistance.
Deliver the placenta 
 
 When visible at the opening of the 
vagina:
 
—hold placenta with both hands and 
turn in one direction.
 
—continue until placenta and all 
membranes are delivered.
 
 Place placenta in bowl/basin.
 
 Check uterine tone immediately.
If heavy bleeding, but placenta is 
not out. Start PPH treatment bundle 
immediately, then move to manual 
removal. We will discuss this more later.

12b

When the placenta is out
Check tone, massage if soft, 
check bleeding
 
 
13

Check tone, massage if soft, check bleeding
A soft uterus is the #1 cause of PPH
• Always check tone immediately after 
the placenta is delivered.
• Monitor and massage the uterus when 
soft to help prevent PPH.
• Uterine tone can change quickly. 
• Check the uterus at least every 15 min 
for the first hour after birth.
Assessing tone
• A hard uterus feels like your forehead 
and does not need massage.
• A soft uterus feels like the tip of your 
nose and needs massage.
• The uterus should be firm at midline, 
and approximately level or below the 
umbilicus.
Soft uterus
• If the fundus rises, is off to the side or 
becomes soft again:
 
—it may be full of clots
 
—the bladder may be full.
• Massaging helps contract and expels 
blood clots.
• Encourage frequent urination. A full 
bladder may slow uterine contraction. 
 
 Place hand on abdomen around the 
umbilicus to find the uterus.
 
 Check – it should feel like your forehead.
If soft
 
 Firmly rub the top of the uterus, 
wrapping towards the back.
 
 Guard the uterus with your other hand 
while you massage.
 
 Massage to cause a contraction and 
express clots.
 
 Sweep blood and clots into the 
measurement tool. 
 
 Encourage urination.
 
 Catheterize if bladder is full and she is 
unable to urinate.
 
 Recheck uterine tone, massage if soft.
 
 Assess and record on the Postpartum 
Monitoring Form.
1. True or false: once the uterus contracts 
or gets hard, it will always stay hard.
 
—False – A uterus can lose tone and 
begin to bleed.
2. Why might a uterus not contract?
 
—There may be retained tissue, a 
ruptured uterus, or the woman’s 
bladder may be full.

After delivering the placenta
• First, ensure good uterine tone and 
no PPH.
• Then check the placenta and

missing lobes or fragments.
• Any retained tissue can cause 
haemorrhage and infection – even a 
piece of membrane.
• If the placenta is not complete, missing 
lobes must be removed manually. We 
will review this later.
Show video Examining the placenta 
(4 min) or demonstrate using the 
simulator.
 
 Cup the placenta in your hands, 
maternal side facing up.
 
 Check if the lobes fit together and if any 
are missing.
 
 Hold the placenta upside down by the 
cord. 
 
 With opposite hand, spread out the 
membranes to recreate the sac.
 
 Check the membranes for missing 
pieces.
1. If a piece of the placenta or membrane 
stays in the uterus, why does the woman 
bleed more? 
 
—The uterus cannot contract to 
squeeze the blood vessels and stop 
the bleeding.

Check for tears and repair
• 
• Trauma results in tears – another cause 
of PPH.
• If there is bleeding but the uterus is firm 
and the placenta is complete, tears are 
likely the cause.
• Assess gently and thoroughly – tears can 
be difficult to see.
• The risk of bleeding from tears increases 
in case of:
 
—female genital mutilation or cutting
 
—episiotomy
 
—large baby
 
—augmented or obstructed labour
 
—assisted vaginal birth.
Act within your scope of practice. Refer 
to more experienced health workers when 
tears are beyond your scope.
Demonstrate using the simulator and a 
volunteer as the woman.
 
 Obtain consent and ensure privacy.
 
 Explain your actions and be gentle.
Assess for tears
 
 Ensure good lighting.
 
 Gently wipe away blood and clots from 
the vagina and cervix.
 
 Assess the extent of the tears and 
related bleeding.
 
 Respond based on your scope of 
Manage tears
 
 Follow local protocols.
 
 Apply firm pressure with a sterile gauze.
 
 Continue pressure until bleeding stops, 
or suturing starts.
 
 Do not place soaked gauze in the tool.
1. How do you manage serious lacerations 
in your facility?
2. Is someone available at all times to

After one hour

1. Why should you keep woman and baby 
under your care for at least an hour?
1. Why should you assess and record 
repeatedly, as you give care?
 
—Her status can change quickly – check 
often to respond fast.
 
—To see trends and diagnose PPH early.
 
—To refer to the record when 
communicating with team.
 
—So team members can quickly see the 
woman’s status and know what care 
has been given.
2. If Mrs. A’s BP is 110/74 and her pulse is 
90, what is her SI?
 
—90/110 = SI 0.81 = <1.
3. If Mrs. B’s BP is 110/74 and her pulse is 
112, what is her SI?
 
—112/110 = SI 1.02 = >1.
4. Which woman has a SI that is a warning 
sign and why?
 
—Mrs. B because her pulse is higher 
than her systolic BP, meaning her 
SI is >1.

MODULE 3 
Treatment with the PPH bundle
M

E
Diagnose and treat PPH early
PPH bundle
min

• Many deaths from PPH at both vaginal 
and caesarean births can be prevented 
with:
 
—prompt recognition with the 
objective blood loss measuring tool 
and warning signs/vital signs 
 
—prompt treatment with the PPH 
bundle.
Early diagnosis 
Early diagnosis is the first step and it 
begins with you. 
• Blood loss ≥ 300 mL with any other 
warning sign, or
• Blood loss ≥ 500 mL, or
• Clinical judgment.
If PPH, call for help and start 
treatment bundle
• A clinical bundle is a set of interventions 
that, when given together, improves 
outcomes.
• For the PPH clinical bundle, use the 
mnemonic MOTIVE to remember the 
interventions: 
 
—massage the uterus to stimulate 
contractions 
 
—oxytocic (uterotonic) drugs to 
stimulate contractions 
 
—TXA prevents clots from breaking 
down 
 
—IV access/fluids 
 
—examine to find the cause of 
After the PPH bundle, escalate care if 
bleeding persists, the cause is unclear, or 
cannot be managed.
When the woman gave birth 
elsewhere, you may not know the 
amount of blood lost. Rely on your 
assessment and clinical judgment. 
When in doubt, treat.
Practice
Taking a “quick pulse”
• Count your heart beat at your neck or 
wrist for 6 seconds, using a watch or 
clock. 
• Multiply this number by 10 for the quick 
pulse rate.
1. If a woman has lost <500 mL of blood but 
>300 mL, what are the warning signs that 
would have you diagnose PPH and begin 
treatment? 
 
—Pulse >100, or systolic BP <100, or 
diastolic BP <60 or a SI >1 (pulse > 
systolic BP)
 
—Rapid blood flow, large clots, history 
of anaemia.

21

When you diagnose PPH
• Shout for help and emergency 
equipment and medication.
• Do a rapid assessment for shock. 
• Explain your actions to the woman and 
her companion.
• Communicate with the health team and 
establish roles.
Tools for team communication
• Good team communication saves lives.
• It helps reduce errors, especially when 
calling for help or handing over care.
• We will review two techniques: 
 
—SBAR to present a clinical case to 
team members in a structured way
 
—closed-loop communication to 
confirm clear understanding. 
1. SBAR 
Act out the following example explaining 
what the letters stand for. 
• Situation: What’s happening now?
 
—Please, come help me with Mariam! 
She gave birth an hour ago and is 
now bleeding heavily.
• Background: What led up to this?
 
—She had a normal bith, but has 
lost 350 mL of blood. She received 
oxytocin after birth.
• Assessment: What do you think is 
going on? 
 
—I think she may be having PPH. Her 
pulse is 110, BP 90/60, and the uterus 
is soft.
• Recommendation: What do you need?
 
—I need you to help me. We need to 
start the PPH bundle so please bring 
the emergency trolley.
2. Closed-loop communication
Ask two participants to act out the 
example of closed-loop on page 10 of the 
Provider Guide. 
Practice
Read with participants the SBAR case on 
page 11 of the Provider Guide.
1. Individual reflection (2 min)
 
—Review the SBAR template in the 
Provider Guide.
 
—Based on the case, how would you 
use it when calling a colleague?
2. Share-out (5 min)
 
—One participant demonstrates to the 
larger group how they would use the 
tool to communicate this case.
• Do you have an emergency trolley or 
kit? If not, how could you create one? 
• What was easy or difficult about using 
SBAR and closed-loop?
• How could this help in real 
emergencies?
• Why is it important to establish roles?

21b

22

Starting the PPH bundle
• Administer all interventions, even if the 
woman improves after only one or two. 
• The order does not matter.
• Aim to finish all interventions in 15 min. 
Massage the uterus 
• To cause contraction, expel blood and 
clots, assess for distended bladder. 
• If alone, massage first, then move on. 
Give oxytocin/uterotonic 
• Give oxytocin 10 IU IV:
 
—diluted in 100–500 mL of crystalloid 
fluids as fast as possible (preferable to 
avoid hypotension)
 
—or as bolus over 1–2 min.
• If no IV access:
 
—give oxytocin 10 IU IM or misoprostol 
 
—call for help to start IV.
Give TXA
• 1 g IV over 10 min. Faster administration 
can cause hypotension. 
• TXA and oxytocin can be given in the 
same line, but not in the same bag.
• Do not start TXA if: 
 
—3 h or more since birth
 
—or if there is a contraindication or 
hypersensitivity to TXA, known 
thromboembolic event, renal failure 
or history of convulsions. 
• Use 18 gauge cannula or largest available. 
• Collect blood for: 
 
—bedside haemoglobinometer, or
 
—lab testing for Hb, cross‐match, and 
clotting studies if available.
• Begin infusion of crystalloid fluids NS or 
RL, if not given with oxytocin already.
• If clinically indicated, insert 2nd IV line 
with crystalloid fluids (NS or RL) for fluid 
resuscitation.
Examine for causes
• As you are providing care, notice 
potential causes such as:
 
—atony when you massage
 
—tears as you check blood flow.
• We will review examination shortly.
During and after a caesarean 
section (CS)
• Challenges:
 
—there is often more bleeding
 
—interpreting the haemodynamic 
signs which may be affected by 
anaesthesia.
• Most PPH bundle components are 
already given.
• Use clinical judgment to initiate 
treatment and decide to give TXA.
1. How is the PPH bundle different to your 
current practice?
2. What challenges do you see in this new 
practice?
3. How do you measure blood loss at CS?

22b

 Examine and address 
causes
23

 Examine and address causes
The last E in MOTIVE is for examination.
Once the other interventions in the 
bundle have been started:
• Communicate with the woman and 
companion. Explain respectfully what is 
happening.
• Examine thoroughly to identify and 
address all causes of bleeding.
• Begin with tone and work through 
causes. 
• Record findings and actions.
Examine and address
Tone 
• Recheck frequently that it remains firm.
• Check if fundus is firm, below umbilicus 
and midline.
• If the uterus is soft, massage to improve 
tone and expel clots.
• Assess for full bladder. Encourage 
frequent urination.
• Catheterize the bladder if she cannot 
urinate or the bleeding is heavy.
Tissue 
• Inspect the placenta carefully for 
missing lobes, fragments or membranes.
• Inspect vagina, cervix and uterus to 
remove clots and tissue.
• Remember, if the placenta is adherent, 
suspect accreta and surgery is needed. 
Trauma 
• Check for perineal vaginal and cervical 
tears, and repair.
• Refer if you are unable to do the repair.
• If inverted uterus, replace and follow 
local protocols.
• If you suspect uterine rupture, seek 
advanced care.
Thrombin/coagulopathies 
• If possible, collect blood for bedside or 
lab testing for: 
 
—Hb 
 
—type and cross match 
 
—prothrombin time, partial 
thromboplastin time and platelets
 
—fibrinogen 
 
—coagulopathy. 
Advanced Care Note 
If within your scope of practice and 
training, provide additional care 
per local protocols. If beyond your 
scope of practice, seek advanced care

• Diagnose PPH < 500 mL with hemodynamic 
warning signs.
• Treat PPH with the PPH bundle.

Scenario practice 4
26b

MODULE 4
if bleeding continues
27

The last E in MOTIVE is also for escalation.
• If bleeding: 
 
—is heavy while giving the bundle, or
 
—continues after bundle is complete, 
 
—is more than 1000 mL at any time.
• If a woman:
 
—has extensive trauma or
 
—has uterine inversion or
 
—is hypotensive or unresponsive. 
• If you are unable to identify or manage 
the cause. 
Act fast. The woman’s life is in danger. 
Call for more help 
• There should always be at least two 
health workers during an emergency.
• Request the most senior health worker 
to urgently attend the woman. 
• Always continue monitoring and give 
what treatment you can while waiting 
for help or transfer. 
• Call for the anaesthetist if there is one at 
this facility.
Communicate and assign roles 
• Use SBAR tool to communicate clinical 
status. 
• The most senior health worker leads the 
team and assigns roles.
• Use closed‐loop communication to 
confirm understanding and completion 
of tasks.
Continually assess for shock 
Early signs of shock
• Fast or weak pulse > 100 bpm.
• Systolic BP < 100 mmHg. 
• SI >1 (pulse > systolic BP).
Late signs of shock
• Very low BP and weak pulse.
• Rapid breathing >30 breaths/min.
• Pale skin, including eyelids, mouth, 
palms.
• Sweating.
• Change in mental status – anxiety, 
confusion, unconsciousness.
• Scanty urine output (<30 mL/h). 
If shock – Check ABCs and manage
• Open airway and ensure breathing.
• If not breathing or in cardiac arrest, 
begin resuscitation. 
• Start oxygen at 6–8 L/min.
• Assess circulation – BP and heart rate.
• Insert second IV for crystalloid fluids and 
blood transfusion. 
• Support/increase blood volume.
• Apply NASG if shock or risk of shock. 
• Prepare for blood transfusion.
Advanced care note 
Transfer immediately while still providing 
care if what the woman needs is beyond 
the scope of your facility.

if bleeding continues

27b

If needed
Arrange transfer 
or surgery
28

Arrange transfer or surgery
All facilities should have a formal referral 
protocol, including for internal referrals.
• The woman may need to be transferred:
 
—to another facility or
 
—to the surgical unit in your facility.
Act fast 
• Delay in care is a common reason for 
PPH deaths. 
• Don not wait until she is in shock to 
initiate transfer.
Prepare in advance 
• Transfers may be complicated and delay 
care. 
• Visibly post contact information for 
health workers, facilities, surgical and 
transport teams. 
• Communicate the need for transport 
or surgery to your team and woman as 
soon as possible. 
• Explain to the woman and her family, 
what is happening.
Communicate with referral facility 
or surgical team
• Notify the referral facility or surgical 
team of the transfer. 
• Use SBAR to communicate with the 
referral health worker. 
• Write a note for the receiving facility 
following national guidelines. Include:
 
—assessment
 
—diagnosis
 
—care provided
 
—last vital signs. 
Care before and during transport 
• If available, place NASG before transport. 
• Never leave the woman alone. 
• Continue care during referral and 
transport.
• Ensure all elements of the PPH bundle 
were given, plus the 2nd dose TXA.
• Continue the oxytocin and crystalloid IV 
infusion.
• Monitor and record uterine tone, blood 
flow and loss, pulse and BP.
• Always transfer the baby with the 
woman. Keep them warm.
Minimize bleeding during transfer
• Insert indwelling catheter to keep the 
bladder empty. 
• For bleeding tears you cannot repair: 
continue to apply firm, steady pressure 
with a sterile cloth. 
• Continue massage or bimanual uterine 
compression.
• Use bimanual or aortic compression, as 
needed. 
Advanced Care Note 
If participants have additional training 
and authorization to provide more 
advanced care, they should do so prior to 
and during transport. 
If needed
Arrange transfer 
or surgery
28
28b

If available
 Rapidly apply NASG
29

 Rapidly apply NASG
• The NASG applies pressure to the lower 
body and abdomen.
• It forces blood to the heart, lungs, and 
brain to prevent shock, or stabilize a 
woman in shock.
• NASG does not treat PPH but gives you 
time to seek treatment.
When to use NASG
• Any time there is a delay in care 
– transfer, waiting for blood, surgery, or 
procedures.
• Keep it on during all procedures, 
transport and surgery. 
• Remove per protocol, only when 
bleeding stops and the woman is stable.
Usage tips
• Apply segments with strong pressure, 
but allow breathing in the abdominal 
area.
• It’s faster with two people, but only one 
should handle segments 4, 5, and 6 to 
avoid overtightening.
• Leave the knees exposed for bending.
• For short women, fold segment 1 into 
segment 2 and start from segment 2. 
• Apply the NASG even if the woman is 
unconscious.
Procedures and treatment while 
NASG is in place
• The NASG stretches for checking uterine 
tone and massage.
• It can remain on during vaginal 
procedures and toileting – slide 
segment 4 if needed.
• Leave it on during surgery, but remove 
segments 4, 5, and 6 before incision, 
replacing them afterward.
In your facility, who can:
1. Train staff on cleaning and storage of the 
NASG?
2. Manage NASG transport and 
maintenance between referral and 
referring facilities?
3. Train new health workers on the NASG 
protocol?
If available
 Rapidly apply NASG
29
Before the course day, determine if NASG is available at this 
facility. If it is, check the protocol for timing of use. 
If NASG is not available, skip this page and the next.
29b

Skills practice – NASG
30

Skills practice – NASG
Skills practice
Skip this page if NASG is not available in the participants’ facility.
• Divide participants in groups, with one NASG per group.
• Gather necessary equipment and ensure the NASG is laid out flat.
• Refer to page 33 in the Provider Guide.
2. Demonstrate
Show video Using an anti‐shock garment (9:15 min) or demonstrate 
with help of a volunteer using the checklist on this page.
3. Practise
Allow participants to practise. Use the checklist, also available in 
Provider Guide page 33.
Skills practice checklist
 
 Explain your actions and be gentle.
 
 Assign roles in the team.
Place the woman on the NASG
 
 Roll her onto her side.
 
 Align the top of the NASG at her lowest rib.
 
 Align the pressure ball at the level of umbilicus.
 
 Align the dotted line with her spine.
 
 Roll her to the other side and flatten the garment.
 
 Roll her to her back again.
 
 Close each segment pair, starting from the ankles and ending with 
6th segment.
 
 Use sufficient strength while ensuring the woman can breathe 
normally.
Check fit
 
 Place 1–2 fingers under the top of each closed segment.
 
 Pull up on the fabric, release and listen for a snapping sound.
 
 If no snapping sound, tighten the segment.
 
 Check woman can breathe comfortably.
 
 Loosen segments 5 and 6 if necessary .
Monitoring during use
 
 Continue to check tone, blood loss and flow, pulse and BP, per 
protocol.
 
 Note any signs of shortness of breath or decreased urine output.
Before removal
 
 Ensure the following has happened for at least 2 h:
 
—pulse is 100 bpm or less
 
—systolic BP is 100 mmHg or greater
 
—bleeding is reduced to 50 mL/h or less.
 
 Ensure IV fluids continue.
Removing the NASG
 
 Begin removal by opening ankle segments only.
 
 Wait 15 min and check that:
 
—pulse does not increase more than 20 bpm 
 
—systolic BP does not decrease more than 20 mmHg.
 
 If vitals stable, open next segment pair in order, wait 15 min, then 
check vital signs.
 
 Continue in the same way with remaining segments.
 
 If any vital signs change beyond limits:
 
—quickly re‐secure all segments starting from the last segment 
opened 
 
—check for bleeding source.
After removal
 
 Record procedure and observations in the Postpartum Monitoring 
Form.
 
 Continue to assess and record the woman’s vital signs and 
condition.

Health worker 1
Continue massage, 
catheterize bladder, 
remove clots/debris
31

Continue massage, catheterize bladder, remove clots/debris
There should always be at least two health 
workers during an emergency. The first 
health worker will focus on care at the 
perineum and abdomen. 
Actions include:
1. Communicate with the woman, family 
and team: 
 
—explain what you are doing, and why 
 
—let her know that she may feel 
discomfort. 
2. Massage:
 
—expel clots contract the uterus 
 
—monitor and report uterine tone and 
3. Catheterize the bladder: 
 
—use sterile technique and place a 
catheter to empty the bladder 
 
—ensure no urine goes into the blood 
loss measurement tool. 
4. Remove clots and debris:
 
—ensure cervix is not blocked before 
clearing the uterus 
 
—remove clots and tissue to aid 
contraction and prevent infection. 
Ensure the uterus is clear before 
considering UBT. If you cannot clear the 
uterus, seek advanced care. 
 
 Ensure privacy. Explain to the woman 
what you will do and why.
 
 Catheterize the bladder.
Remove clots and debris from 
the cervix 
 
 Use sterile gloves.
 
 Gently perform a vaginal exam until you 
reach the cervix. It will feel swollen and 
loose.
 
 Check for clots and tissue in the 
cervical os. 
 
 Gently pull them out. 
 
 At the same time, massage the fundus 
with your other hand to assist removal 
and stimulate contractions.
Remove clots and debris from 
the uterus
If the uterus is not firm, and it is within 
your scope of practice. 
 
 Offer pain relief per local protocol, 
before you begin.
 
 Give a single dose of antibiotics:
 
—Ampicillin 2 g or
 
—Cefazolin 1 g IV. 
 
 Wash your hands, use long, sterile 
gloves.
 
 Wrap sterile gauze around your index 
and middle fingers.
 
 Similar to manual removal of placenta:
 
—form the hand into a cone and 
 
—gently guide it into the uterus.
 
 Wipe the interior of the uterus with the 
gauze.
 
 Bring out all debris as you remove your 
hand. 
 
 Ensure you remove all the gauze.
 
 Check uterine tone and massage if soft.

31b

Health worker 2
Start 2nd IV, 
give additional uterotonics, 
repeat TXA, 
assess and record
32

Start second IV, give additional uterotonics and TXA second dose
The second health worker will manage the 
medications, IV and recording. If you are 
alone, you will provide all treatments.
Actions include: 
1. Place a second IV line:
 
—for additional IV fluid
 
—to administer other medications
 
—to allow for blood transfusion 
 
—to allow for additional laboratory 
tests per local protocols.
2. Give additional uterotonics.
3. Repeat TXA.
4. Assess and record every 15 min or 
more often until stable:
 
—tone, blood loss and flow, as reported 
by health worker
 
—pulse and BP.
• Act fast. If bleeding continues, she 
may go into shock and die. Delays are a 
common reason women die from PPH.
Additional uterotonics
The choice of uterotonic should be 
based on availability and health worker’s 
experience.
Oxytocin 
• 20 IU in 1 L crystalloid fluids (NS or RL) IV. 
• Infuse at 40 drops/min over 4 h. 
• Do not give more than 3 L of IV fluids 
with oxytocin in 24 h. 
• Maximum 60 IU in 24 h.
• Consider other uterotonic if oxytocin 
already infusing. 
Ergometrine or ergometrine/oxytocin 
fixed dose
• Ergometrine:
 
—200 μg IV or IM in 15 min
 
—if needed, repeat every 4 h up to 5 
doses (1 mg total) in 24 h.
• Ergometrine/oxytocin fixed dose:
 
—500 μg / 5 IU IM
 
—do not repeat.
• Use either if oxytocin unavailable or not 
effective.
• Do not use either if suspected retained 
placenta or if hypertension cannot be 
ruled out.
Misoprostol
• 800 μg SL – or PR if concerned about 
pyrexia or under anaesthesia.
Do not give heat-stable carbetocin for 
treatment – only for PPH prevention.
TXA second dose 
• 1 g IV over 10 min
• Give if bleeding:
 
—continues more than 30 min after first 
dose 
 
—or restarts within 24 h after first dose.
• Can be given in the same line as 
oxytocin but not mixed in the same IV 
bag. 
Pause and reflect 
If additional uterotonics and TXA fail, 
move quickly to transfer/surgery.
1. If oxytocin fails or is not available, how 
do you choose which uterotonic to give?
 
—Availablilty and health workers 
experience.

33b

Module 5
Advanced interventions 
and post-PPH care
34

By now you have: 
• Completed the PPH bundle. 
• Called for more help, assigned tasks. 
• Inserted a 2nd IV and given extra doses 
of medications.
• Repaired tears, removed the placenta, 
and clots and tissue as needed.
• Applied NASG, if available.
If bleeding continues, consider:
• More than one cause of bleeding.
• Uterine rupture, especially if augmented 
labour or prior CS. 
• Deep vaginal or cervical laceration.
Remember – atony is the most common 
cause of PPH. 
Additional care includes
Start safe blood transfusion
• If the woman has severe or ongoing PPH 
and there is a clinical need.
• Or if the woman is severely anaemic:
 
—Hb <7 g/dl, or
 
—she looks anaemic clinically. 
Repair deep vaginal and cervical tears
• Recheck for vaginal and cervical 
lacerations that might have been 
missed.
• Repair if within your scope, or refer.
Apply bimanual compression 
• As a temporizing measure. 
• Squeeze the uterus to compress vessels, 
decrease blood flow and express clots. 
Insert UBT 
• To compress blood vessels from the 
inside of the uterus. 
Apply aortic compression
• As a temporizing measure. 
• Often done for better visualization 
when repairing a laceration or inserting 
a UBT.
Surgical interventions
These interventions should only be 
conducted by trained health workers.
• When all other methods fail, these 
surgical can interventions address the 
causes of PPH directly: 
 
—uterine compression sutures
 
—uterine or uteroovarian artery 
ligation
 
—subtotal or total hysterectomy.
• See page 51 in the Provider Guide 
for details.
• Prepare for surgery and provide 
additional care in the operating room if:
 
—blood loss >1 L, or
 
—blood loss >500 mL with warning 
signs:
pulse >100 bpm
systolic BP <100 mmHg
diastolic BP <60 mmHg
SI >1.

Advanced interventions 
and post-PPH care

34b

For temporary control of bleeding
35

Act quickly. Do not wait until the woman 
is in shock to compress the uterus.
• Squeeze the uterus between your hands 
to reduce bleeding and buy time for 
medications to work. 
• Bimanual compression can be used 
while awaiting placement of UBT or 
surgery. 
• This is painful, but lifesaving. Inform the 
woman.
• Do not use vaginal packing. It can 
restrict optimal assessment of blood 
loss and cause infection. 
• Show video Uterine compression 
(2:40 min) or demonstrate using the 
simulator.
• Ask participants to practise in pairs and 
provide guidance.
• As facilitator, wear the simulator with 
the baby and placenta delivered. 
Tighten the cervix. 
Prepare
 
 Tell the woman what you are about to 
do, why, and that it will hurt.
 
 Consider pain medication.
 
 Wash hands and put on long sterile 
gloves.
 
 Form the hand into a cone and gently 
guide it into the vagina.
 
 Make a fist against the upper part of the 
vagina and the uterus.
 
 Place the other hand on the abdomen 
at the fundus. 
 
 Compress the uterus between your 
hands for at least 5 min.
 
 After 5 min, slowly remove hand and 
check if bleeding restarts.
 
 If bleeding restarts, resume 
compression.
 
 If no bleeding:
 
—ensure IV infusion with oxytocin 
continues
 
—monitor closely.

 Insert uterine balloon tamponade
• Insert a UBT only after completing the 
PPH bundle and if it fails. 
• Do not place UBT until retained tissue 
and trauma have been ruled out.
• Keep UBT supplies in PPH emergency kit. 
• Consider aortic compression before 
insertion to minimize bleeding for 
better visualization. 
Advanced care note 
Health workers should act within their 
scope of practice. UBT should only be 
placed by health workers specifically 
trained to do so.
• Show video Aortic compression (2:50 
min) and UBT manufacturer video 
if available. Or demonstrate using a 
simulator.
• Use a postpartum uterus model or 
500 mL bottle for practice. 
• Ask participants to practise in pairs and 
provide guidance.
Aortic compression
 
 Ensure the woman is on a firm surface.
 
 Explain the procedure to her.
 
 With thumb tucked, make a fist and 
apply downward pressure on the 
abdominal aorta – just above and to the 
left of the umbilicus.
 
 Palpate the femoral pulse with your 
other hand. 
 
 If still palpable, increase pressure.
UBT insertion prep 
 
 Check and remove any retained clots 
and tissue.
 
 Ensure deep tears are repaired.
 
 Ensure empty bladder.
 
 Administer antibiotics (ampicillin 2 g or 
cefazolin 1 g IV).
 
 Explain the procedure to the woman 
and ensure privacy.

instructions.

 Leave the UBT in place per 
manufacturer’s instructions.
UBT removal 
 
 Remove per manufacturer’s instructions.
 
 Monitor closely.
 
 Assess and record tone, blood loss and 
flow, pulse and BP.

36b

Repair deep tears
37

Repair deep tears
• Tears that cause PPH are most often deep 
vaginal or cervical tears.
• Cervical tears often occur at 3 and 9 
o’clock.
• Bleeding from a tear may be slow, heavy, 
or spurting from an artery. 
• Seek advanced care if repair does not 
stop bleeding – surgery may be required. 
• Show video Cervical tears (5 min) or 
demonstrate. Then practise.
Vaginal tears – Identify 
 
 Ensure privacy and inform the woman.
 
 Ensure good lighting. 
 
 Give IV sedative per protocol. Do not give 
if in shock.
 
 Wash hands and wear sterile gloves.
 
 Clean perineum, vulva, and vagina with 
antiseptic solution.
 
 Gently separate the labia and assess 
completely.
 
 Wrap fingers in gauze and press on the 
vaginal floor to expose the entire sulcus.
Vaginal tears – Repair 
 
 Draw 10 mL of 1% lignocaine into syringe.
 
 Insert the needle from the bottom to the 
apex on one side of the tear.
 
 Withdraw plunger to ensure needle is not 
in a blood vessel.
 
 Inject medication as needle is withdrawn.
 
 Repeat on other side of the tear. Wait 2 
min for effect.
 
 Repair in 2 layers:
 
—interrupted sutures to close deep layer 
first
 
—continuous suturing starting just 
beyond the apex to close the vaginal 
mucosa.
 
 Avoid suturing into rectum.
 
 Review wound care and hygiene.
Cervical tears – Identify 
 
 Have an assistant apply fundal pressure 
to help visualize the cervix.
 
 Use a sponge forceps to grasp cervix 
at 12 o’clock position and another at 3 
o’clock.
 
 Inspect between the forceps for tears.
 
 Move the first forceps to 6 o’clock and 
inspect again.
 
 Continue to rotate forceps until full cervix 
is inspected.
Cervical tears – Repair
 
 Gently hold both forceps in one hand.
 
 Use 0 Vicryl suture.
 
 Place first suture above the tear.
 
 Close tear with continuous suture.
Repair deep tears
37
• Follow local protocols on laceration repair.
• Participants can use foam blocks or towels as tear repair 
simulators. Encourage participants to create their own 
simulators for ongoing practice.
37b

When bleeding stops
 Provide post‐PPH care
38

 Provide post‐PPH care
Special care after PPH 
• Monitor closely until stable.
• Assess and record tone, blood loss and 
flow, pulse and BP: 
 
—at least every 15 min until stable 
 
—then every 30 min for 2 h
 
—then as per routine.
• A maintenance infusion of oxytocin 
10–20 IU in 500–1000 mL may be 
needed in the 4 h after treatment to 
prevent recurrence.
• Increase PO hydration and remove 
urinary catheter.
• Decrease oxygen per protocol.
• Support breastfeeding.
• Ensure the woman’s record is complete 
with final measured blood loss, timing 
of escalation, all assessments and 
interventions.
When stable
• Repeat lab tests – FBC/Hb per protocol.
• Gradually increase physical activity.
Home readiness 
• Before discharge, ensure:
 
—normal vital signs, urine output, and 
mental state 
 
—no dizziness with walking 
 
—she can care for herself and her baby 
 
—no sign of infection.
• Continue or begin antibiotics per 
protocol. 
Discharge instructions 
Counsel the woman and her family
• Ensure rest and good nutrition to 
support breastfeeding and recovery.
• Teach signs of anaemia, bleeding, and 
infection, and to seek care right away. 
• Provide routine postpartum care 
including family planning. 
• Counsel on the risk of PPH in future and 
importance of a facility birth. 
• Recommend non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs or paracetamol for 
pain relief. 
• Plan follow up for care at 48 h, 10 days, 
and 6 weeks. 
In case of anaemia
• If Hb was less than 7 g/dl:
 
—provide blood transfusion and 
consider IV iron
 
—do not discharge until Hb >7 g/dl.
• If Hb was 7–11 g/dl discharge with at 
least 3 months of:
 
—iron supplement 120 mg and 
 
—folic acid 400 μg daily. 
Instructions in case of perineal tears 
• Wash the perineum gently front to back, 
twice daily and after bowel movements.
• Change pads frequently. 
• Wash hands before and after self‐care.
Debrief after PPH
• PPH can be a traumatic experience 
– for the woman, her family and the 
healthcare team. 
• To learn how to debrief and support 
each other, review page 53 in the 
Provider Guide with your team. 
When bleeding stops
 Provide post-PPH care
38

MODULE 6
Ongoing practice and 
quality improvement
39

Module 6: Ongoing practice and quality improvement
Low Dose High Frequency
• LDHF is an approach for training:
 
—on‐site
 
—hands‐on
 
—with the whole team.
• It ensures continuous improvement, 
better retention of skills, and sustainable 
behavioural change.
Key Points of LDHF
• Competency focused on mastering 
clinical decision‐making, essential skills 
and behaviours.
• Case‐based training with simulations 
and hands‐on practice.
• Team and facility‐based to support 
multidisciplinary teamwork.
• Brief ongoing activities after the initial 
course:
 
—brief skills practice and drills
 
—quality improvement activities
 
—based on activities outlined in the 
Provider Guide
 
—led by peers selected from your 
facility. 
• Measuring quality of care indicators, 
clinical performance, and outcomes 
to identify areas for improvement 
guided by local needs and adaptation:
 
—uterotonic use for prevention
 
—facility use of simulation and drills
 
—presence of formal protocols for 
PPH prevention, treatment, blood 
transfusion and referral
 
—PPH cases, severe PPH cases (>1000 
mL) cases treated, and deaths from 
PPH.
Have health workers turn to the table of 
contents in the Provider Guide to review 
practice sessions.
• What do you think you need to practise 
at your facility?
• Do you do regular drills at your facility 
already?

39b

 
 
The Bleeding after birth training 
course aims to translate standards into 
care. It incorporates the latest WHO 
recommendations related to PPH1,2 and 
includes links to key references and 
resources for training. 
www.who.int/tools/bleeding-after-birth
Course development methods. The development of this training 
product followed a rigorous, evidence-based, and iterative process. 
The training package was validated using the Kirkpatrick framework, 
assessing feasibility, acceptability, changes in provider performance, and 
improvements in health outcomes. The materials and teaching methods 
are grounded in adult learning principles and clinical best practices, 
ensuring relevance and effectiveness in real-world settings. Beta versions 
of the package were piloted in Afghanistan, Democratic Republic of 
the Congo, Guinea, India, Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria, United Republic of 
Tanzania and Zambia with adaptations made based on feedback and 
implementation learnings from these contexts. The training package was 
used in the EMOTIVE trial, providing robust evidence for its effectiveness 
and impact on maternal and newborn health outcomes. The development 
process involved collaboration with global health experts and institutions 
to ensure alignment with international standards and contextual relevance.
Declaration of interest. All external experts signed declaration of interest 
to WHO, disclosing any potential conflicts of interest that might influence 
or could reasonably be perceived to influence their objectivity and 
independence in relation to the guide’s content. WHO thoroughly reviewed 
each declaration and determined that none posed an actual or reasonably 
perceived conflict of interest concerning any aspect of the course.
